title: Locker room at Montreal’s Olympic sports complex 'falling apart' just months after reno
summary: Less than a year after a multimillion-dollar revitalization of the aging locker room at Montreal’s Complexe Sportif Claude-Robillard, athletes say they've had to navigate cold or broken showers,…

image.caption: Since the Complexe Sportif Claude-Robillard locker rooms reopened to the public in March, users report issues with plumbing such as toilet water running hot, showers running cold as well as leaks from the ceilings. (Douglas Gelevan/ CBC)

blocks.text: Montreal

Less than a year after a multimillion-dollar revitalization of the aging locker room at Montreal’s Complexe Sportif Claude-Robillard, athletes say they've had to navigate cold or broken showers, water fountains with undrinkable hot water and crumbling tiling.
City acknowledges issues with $61.4M interior renovation phase of Complexe Sportif Claude-Robillard
Hot water in the drinking fountains. Showers running cold. Crumbling tiles. Water leaking from the ceiling.
Less than a year after a multimillion-dollar revitalization of the aging locker room at Montreal’s Complexe Sportif Claude-Robillard, athletes are unimpressed with the results.
“I couldn’t believe that so quickly, so fast it was all coming apart,” said Mara Do Santos, who swims in a masters club at Claude-Robillard three days a week.
Émilie Masson, another swimmer with the same group, was most perplexed by hot water in the toilets.
“It's like, 'Wow. Who didn’t do his job?'”
Many of the new showers were taped off and out of order when CBC visited the locker room on Nov. 6. (Douglas Gelevan/CBC)

The locker room at the facility built for the 1976 Olympics closed in August 2024, when the city launched its latest interior phase of an overall $166-million project to modernize the entire complex. It reopened in March 2026.
During CBC’s visit on Nov. 6, at least seven showers were closed and marked “out of order.”
There was also evidence of several leaks in the new ceiling.
In addition to the significant plumbing issues, CBC also noted cosmetic problems such as tiles coming off of walls, hooks missing from their anchors in the changing rooms and rust around the drains.
“It’s brand new — literally,” Do Santos says.
Parts of Montreal's Claude-Robillard sports complex falling apart after $61M refresh
Olympic legacy
The Complexe Sportif Claude-Robillard was originally built for the 1976 Olympic Games when it hosted events such as handball and waterpolo.
It continues to be an important training facility for many Olympic hopefuls in sports like swimming, diving, and track and field.
“This is a top notch sports facility that we have to keep,” Do Santos says.
CBC found several spots in the new ceiling that showed evidence of water damage. (Douglas Gelevan/CBC)
The renovation project to modernize Claude-Robillard was first announced in 2016.
A $61.4-million interior renovations phase that included the locker room and pool mechanical systems began in 2024. Work on the overall project is expected to continue in stages through 2029.
But Masson says that if the quality of work on the locker room is any indication of what's to come, taxpayers should be worried.
Only months after reopening, some tiles are already falling off the walls inside the locker room at the Complexe Sportif Claude-Robillard (Douglas Gelevan/CBC)
“The big renovation itself is not done. The locker room, apparently, it's done. But it’s falling apart,” Masson says. “Can’t we have a good quality that will last?”
The City of Montreal did not respond to CBC’s request for an interview.

But in an email, city spokesperson Kim Nantais Desormiers acknowledged there are issues and went on to say that the city is following up with contractors and subcontractors that worked on the locker room.
A shower grate is showing signs of rust only months after the newly renovated locker room in Complexe Sportif Claude-Robillard reopened to the public. (Douglas Gelevan/CBC)
Problems with pool renovations
Swimmers told CBC the issues with the interior renovations extend to the Olympic-sized pool where they train.
Like the locker room, it was also closed in August 2024. Do Santos says the problems began as soon as it reopened in November 2025.
She said the new movable bulkhead, a kind of floating bridge, would not stay in place.
At one point, her swim team was forced to improvise and use their own ratchet straps to fix it into position, she said.

Émilie Masson, left, and Mara Do Santos, right, use the pool and locker room at Claude-Robillard three times a week and are frustrated to see so many issues come up with the newly renovated spaces. (Charles Contant/CBC)
There are also ongoing issues with the filtration system. The swimmers say the water in the pool is cloudy. The city says it's working to resolve that problem.

In another email to CBC, Nantais Desormiers added that the general contractor responsible for the pool and the locker room will “handle any repairs covered by the applicable warranties” and that all other work will be carried out by the city's municipal maintenance crews.
At this point, no additional costs are anticipated, she says.
Investigation finds breach of municipal regulations
This isn’t the first time the renovations at the sports complex have caused friction.
The office of Montreal's inspector general looked into how the contract for the swimming pool was awarded after receiving a tip from a whistleblower in August 2024.

In a June 2026 report, the office found breaches of municipal regulations by the engineering consulting firm GBI Experts-Conseils Inc. It also highlighted oversight shortcomings within the city's property management department (SGPI).

GBI was awarded an $11.5-million professional services contract in 2022. The investigation concluded that GBI violated regulations by appointing a project manager who was not qualified and that the subsequent call to tenders was compromised and not a fair process.

Mireille Beaudin, director of strategic consulting services for GBI, said in a statement to CBC the company strongly disputes the report’s findings and that it is committed to the “highest ethical and professional standards.”
Work continues at Complexe Sportif Claude-Robillard. A $61.4-million phase of interior renovations began in 2024 that included the locker room and pool mechanical systems. (Douglas Gelevan/CBC)
The inspector general recommended the city impose a $100,000 fine on GBI — the maximum authorized — and that the SGPI reform its vetting processes.
The inspector general says the city has yet to move forward on its recommendations or fine GBI.
City spokesperson Nantais Desormiers says the issue is before the executive council.
Beaudin added that GBI had no part in recruiting the contractors that worked on the locker room.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Douglas Gelevan is a national award-winning journalist who works in the CBC Montreal investigative and enterprise journalism unit. Doug is also the host of CBC Montreal Weekend News.
